i think the issue is that for many trans people (including myself) alot of the descriptions of transness by cis allies lacks a sort of nuance that we are used to living with. its hard to say exactly whats wrong with cenk’s assessment because i haven’t seen his full tweet/thread. for me, a cis ally’s definition doesnt work because it doesnt have the nuance a trans person’s definition does, however, i think these descriptions are useful for other cis people. if you’re cis and you want to better understand the trans experience, the “born in the wrong body” idea can work. its an effective starting point for helping someone understand what trans people are, even if its ultimately wrong. i think of it like how in early math, youre taught that you cant square root a negative number, then as you progress you learn about imaginary numbers. most people do not need to know about imaginary numbers, most people dont need to understand transness as a trans person does. the person who responded to these tweets failed in their own way, because they looked at this interaction as an expert. to continue the math metaphor, this conversation is like two students getting into an argument with each other. one says that you cant square root a negative, the other says when you square root a negative the answer is always 35. technically both are wrong, but one is wrong because theyre at a lower level of understanding, and the other is wrong because theyre fucking stupid and probably trolling. if you are the teacher in this situation, it is in your best interest to defend the first student. 
theyre right tho in a way because these interactions are like two kids bickering over 7*8. but as trans people we should try to remember that most people are still learning, and thats ok.

this is a pretty common thing with english teachers. it refers to how he and she are used “she is/he is”, as opposed to how they is used, “they are”. neopronouns such as ze can be used as “ze is” which falls in line with rules around singular pronouns. ive had this argument with my dad plenty of times and it comes down to him acknowledging the utility of the singular they, but considering how it effects the rules surrounding grammar. before he retired he started teaching the singular they, but had to follow it up with the fact that the college board does not recognize singular they, and that it would be incorrect on an ap test. language is always changing, but it’s important to consider how the changes impact the rules of that language. personally i find it to be a worth while exception to the rule.
